newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Aeroflot Boeing buy seen bad for Russian engines.
newsitem.headline: Aeroflot Boeing buy seen bad for Russian engines.

text.p: Sales of Russian-made planes are being grounded by problems with domestic engines, analysts and executives said on Wednesday, after flagship carrier Aeroflot announced it would add new Boeings to its fleet.

"It is a move against Russian engine producers," United City Bank aircraft industry analyst Patricia Isayeva said of Aeroflot's recent decision to buy 10 737-400 short-medium range aircraft from the Boeing Co.
"It is the logical move for Russian plane producers (to seek Western engines)."

Aeroflot, which has decided to buy the 737s, costing $25-30 million each, for use on domestic and foreign routes starting next year, joined Air Ukraine and Russia's Transaero, in recently announcing or concluding deals for Western planes.
Aeroflot officials gave mixed explanations for the choice.
Chief executive Yevgenny Shaposhnikov said Russian domestic engines were inadequate, Interfax news agency reported.

Aeroflot at its own expense has had to change 48 Perm Motors engines on its fleet of six long range Ilyushin 96-300 aircraft since the beginning of 1995, Aeroflot deputy director for technical issues Gennady Anikayev told Reuters.
The planes altogether have a total of 24 engines.
Anikayev said Aeroflot chose the Boeings because there are no Russian competitors in its class.
But Perm Motors, which supplies the Tupolev 204 with engines, said the Russian aircraft was a competitor.
Though Anikayev says Perm engines are improving in quality, a 1995 preliminary agreement between Aeroflot and Ilyushin may serve as a model for Russian plane makers eager for sales.
Aeroflot agreed to buy 20 Ilyushin long-range planes -- with U.S. engines.

Anikayev said the U.S. engines would extend the range of the Russian craft by 2,000 km, though Perm Motors chief engineer Ivan Bashkatov said his engines could compete with the foreign engines, even on flights from Russia to South America.
The deal has already seen at least one imitator.
Egypt's Kato group on August 31 said it had ordered Rolls Royce plc engines for 13 Tupolev-204 aircraft which it will buy, a combination Isayeva said would hearten passengers.
She said a safe image was important for Aeroflot.
"Aeroflot has to do something to protect its image. They need any good planes that don't crash," she said, adding that competition with Russian rival Transaero had become fierce.
She said Western engines were the strongest medicine Aeroflot could afford against crashes.
But AO Permskiye Motory, which says its engines perform to specification and can compete with Western models, adds that Russian carriers prefer leasing planes.
"The biggest problem is not that Russian engines are worse but that the Russian companies are not in good enough financial condition to buy Russian planes," Bashkatov said by telephone.
Aeroflot is buying the 737s but will not pay the entire price tag at once, the company has said.
But Isayeva said Russian aircraft makers should begin making contact with foreign engine manufacturers, as in the Ilyushin deal, where testing is already under way.
"A company buying Russian planes with Western engines -- it is not that bad."
